articles.title: Getting to Know Raga: A 5-Minute Tour
articles.summary: A quick guide to using Raga: from logging your first weight to reading trends and keeping your streak.
articles.content_md:
## What does Raga actually do?

Raga is a BMI calculator with history, trend charts, and weigh-in reminders. The idea is simple: you just log your weight regularly, and Raga does the math, stores the data, and presents it in a way that's easy to read. No drama, no judgment.

## The Calculate tab: your starting point

This is where it all begins. Enter your height and weight, tap Calculate BMI, and you instantly get your result: your BMI number, a colored gauge, and its category. Want to save it? Tap Save to history. You can also create multiple profiles — for family members, say — and switch the active profile with the chips at the top.

## The History tab: where the story lives

A single scale reading tells you nothing, but a string of readings over weeks tells you a lot. In the History tab you can see your weight chart, switch time ranges (7 days to all time), and read automatic insights like averages, upward or downward trends, and estimated weekly pace.

## The Health tab: the numbers behind the scenes

This tab calculates three things from your data: BMR (the energy your body burns at complete rest), daily calorie needs based on activity level, and the ideal weight range for your height. Important: these are all ESTIMATES from general formulas, not medical verdicts. Treat them as a starting point for discussion, not a final conclusion.

## The Streak, Arena, and Profile tabs

Streak tracks your weekly weigh-in consistency and the weight goal you've set. Arena is a community leaderboard for logged-in users who opt in (opt-in defaults to off — your data stays private). Profile holds your unit, theme, reminder, and cloud backup settings.

## Tips for honest data

Weigh yourself under the same conditions every time: in the morning, after using the bathroom, before eating, in similar clothing. Log regularly, and don't get emotional over one weird reading — look at the trend.

## Your data is yours

Raga has no ads and doesn't sell data. All your entries are stored on your phone first, and the app works fully offline. If you want, there's an optional cloud backup to keep your data safe when you switch phones, complete with a backup code that only you hold.

## Where to start?

If this is your first time opening the app: finish onboarding (name, height, starting weight), log one weigh-in to get your first number, and don't rush to set a goal. Spend a week getting a feel for the rhythm. You can set a weight goal later in the Streak tab when you're ready, and change it anytime.

articles.title: How to Read the BMI Gauge Without Panicking
articles.summary: What the colors and numbers on Raga's BMI gauge mean — plus one important thing: BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.
articles.content_md:
## Where does the number come from?

The gauge in Raga shows your Body Mass Index (BMI): your weight in kilograms divided by the square of your height in meters. For example, 70 kg at 1.70 m gives 70 divided by (1.70 × 1.70), about 24.2. Raga calculates this automatically every time you log.

## The colors and categories

The gauge uses the WHO classification for adults:

- Below 18.5: underweight
- 18.5–24.9: normal
- 25–29.9: overweight
- 30 and above: obesity

Each range has its own color so you can read it at a glance. These categories are population screening benchmarks, not labels stamped on your forehead.

## What the gauge does NOT tell you

This is the most important part. The gauge doesn't know your body composition — it can't tell muscle from fat. It doesn't know your age, your health history, or the fat around your belly. Two people with the same gauge number can be in very different shape.

## How to use the gauge healthily

Use the gauge as a compass, not a judge. If the number sits outside the normal range and stays there for weeks, that's a signal to dig deeper — read the BMI limitations article in BMI Academy, for instance, or talk to a health professional. One weird reading now and then? Ignore it, watch the trend.

## A way to think about it

Say the gauge shows 27, the overweight category. The healthy response isn't panic or an instant crash diet. Instead: first, check whether this number is consistent over several weeks or just an occasional blip. Second, look at the bigger picture — waist circumference, how active you are, health history. Third, if the number persists, use it as material for a conversation with a professional.

## When the number deserves to be taken seriously

One category above normal is not a verdict, but if your BMI is 30 or above and stays there, or keeps climbing for months, it deserves to be taken seriously. Not by blaming yourself, but by getting the right help: a doctor, a nutritionist, or simply starting with the small habits covered in the Healthy Habits category.

articles.title: Reading the Trend Chart: One Number Tells You Nothing
articles.summary: Daily weight ups and downs are normal. What matters is the direction of the trend, not today's number.
articles.content_md:
## Why daily numbers lie

Your weight can swing 1–2 kg in a single day, and that's normal. The causes are trivial things: drinking a lot, salty food last night, digestion, or for some people, hormonal cycles. None of that means you suddenly got fatter or thinner in 24 hours.

## The rules of weighing

To make your data comparable, keep conditions consistent: weigh in the morning, after the bathroom, before eating or drinking, in similar clothing. You don't have to do it every day — once a week, same day and time, is good enough for most people.

## How to read the chart in Raga

In the History tab, switch the time range and watch the direction of the line, not the individual dots. A line slowly descending over weeks means your effort is working, even if some dots spike upward along the way. Raga also shows averages and weekly pace so you don't have to guess.

## When to be cautious

Watch out for drastic, unintentional changes — for example, weight dropping or rising a lot in a short time with no change in eating or activity. That's not about dieting; it's a signal to consult a health professional. A healthy trend is slow and steady, not dramatic.

## Weekly averages: the simple trick

If daily numbers make you overthink, try this: weigh three times a week under the same conditions, then look at the average. A weekly average is far more stable and honest than any single daily reading. Compare this week's average with last week's — that's where the real trend is.

## Don't chase the daily number

The most common mistake: seeing the scale up almost a kilo this morning and punishing yourself by barely eating all day. That's like driving while staring at the rear-view mirror — your reactions are always late and pointed the wrong way. Decisions about eating should come from weekly trends, not one number this morning.

## Keep the context too

A number without context is easy to misread. If you were sick, sleep-deprived, or had a week full of food events, note it — Raga stores your history as it is, and context helps you re-read the chart months later without blaming yourself for a messy week.

articles.title: Streaks and Consistency: Play the Long Game
articles.summary: Streaks in Raga aren't about being perfect every day — they're about coming back every time you slip.
articles.content_md:
## Why consistency wins

Lasting weight change almost always comes from small habits repeated over and over, not from one heroic week. Logging your weight, walking regularly, sleeping enough — these boring things quietly reshape your trend chart. The Streak in Raga is designed to celebrate that boring stuff.

## Missing a day isn't failure

One day (or one week) missed doesn't erase your progress. What destroys it isn't the miss — it's deciding to quit entirely because you feel you've failed. If your streak breaks, that's fine. Log again today, and your new streak starts at one.

## Process goals, not just outcome goals

An outcome goal is, say, getting down to 65 kg. A process goal is weighing every Sunday morning and walking 30 minutes three times a week. The outcome isn't fully in your control; the process is. Raga helps with both: weight goals in the Streak tab, and the weigh-in streak as your process goal.

## How to use streaks without stress

Treat the streak as a friendly reminder, not a strict boss. If looking at your streak makes you anxious, turn off the reminders in Profile for a while — there's no punishment. Raga keeps your data, and you can come back whenever you're ready. A healthy relationship with data starts with a healthy relationship with yourself.

## The never-miss-twice rule

There's a popular rule among habit builders: you may miss once, but never twice in a row. Missing once is life — overtime, family events. Missing twice starts becoming a new pattern. This isn't a medical law, just a way of thinking that helps many people get back on track without drama.

## Celebrate the small stuff

Your brain needs proof that the effort matters. Eight weeks of streaks, one month of consistent logging, the first time you dared to look at the chart — all worth celebrating, even if the numbers haven't moved yet. Raga celebrates your milestones through the weekly Wrapped; you can celebrate them your own way too. Just one rule: don't celebrate by quitting.

articles.title: What BMI Is (and Isn't)
articles.summary: Body Mass Index: a simple formula that's useful for screening — not your personal health report card.
articles.content_md:
## The formula is simple

BMI (Body Mass Index) is your weight in kilograms divided by the square of your height in meters. One formula, no expensive equipment, calculable anywhere. That simplicity is exactly what makes it both popular and limited.

## The categories (for adults)

WHO uses these cutoffs for adults:

- Below 18.5: underweight
- 18.5–24.9: normal
- 25–29.9: overweight
- 30 and above: obesity

These cutoffs come from large population datasets and are used worldwide so data can be compared across countries.

## A brief history

The formula was born in the 1830s from Belgian mathematician Adolphe Quetelet. It was never designed to judge an individual's health — it was meant to study the average human body across populations. That fact matters: from day one, BMI has been a population statistics tool.

## What BMI is for

BMI is useful as a cheap, fast first screening step. For researchers and policymakers, it gives a big-picture view of population weight trends. For you, it's a starting point — a signal to pay attention, not a conclusion.

## What BMI is not for

BMI is not a diagnosis. It doesn't directly measure your body fat, doesn't know your muscle mass, and doesn't account for your age. Judging someone's health from BMI alone is like judging a book by its page count — there's information in it, but the story is incomplete.

## Why it's still used today

Despite all its limits, BMI survives for three reasons: it's cheap (no equipment needed), fast (one formula), and standard (data can be compared across regions and years). For large-scale initial screening, that combination is hard to beat. Problems arise when a screening tool gets used as the final verdict.

## BMI in Raga

In this app, BMI is the front door, not the whole house. Raga calculates it automatically, shows it on the gauge, then invites you to look further: trends over time, estimated calorie needs, and educational articles like the one you're reading. Think of BMI as the opening sentence of a conversation about your body — not the conclusion.

articles.title: The Limits of BMI You Need to Know
articles.summary: BMI can't tell muscle from fat — and that's just one of its several limitations.
articles.content_md:
## Muscle vs fat: its biggest problem

A kilogram of muscle and a kilogram of fat weigh the same on the scale, but BMI treats them identically. Athletes or regular strength trainers can land in the overweight category despite low body fat and good fitness. Conversely, a sedentary person can have a normal BMI with high body fat. BMI is blind to body composition.

## Age plays a role

As we age, muscle mass tends to decline while body fat can increase — at the same weight. So the same BMI number at 25 and 65 can tell very different stories. BMI also wasn't designed for pregnant women or growing children.

## Not all populations are the same

Research shows the link between BMI and health risk can differ across ethnic groups. Some Asian countries, for example, use slightly lower cutoffs because metabolic risk appears at smaller BMIs. The global benchmark is a useful starting point, but not a sacred number for everyone.

## Belly fat goes undetected

Two people with identical BMIs can store fat in different places — and fat around the belly (visceral) is linked to higher risk than fat on the hips or thighs. BMI sees none of this distribution.

## The takeaway

Use BMI alongside other indicators: waist circumference, fitness, blood pressure, blood sugar, and most importantly, a health professional's assessment. One number is never enough to conclude anything about someone's health — including yours.

## So what should you use instead?

The honest answer: a combination. BMI for a rough picture, waist circumference for fat distribution, and for a fuller picture, clinical checks like blood pressure, blood sugar, and lipid profiles. There is no single magic number that sums up your health — and that's actually good news: your health isn't determined by any single number.

## A healthier way to think

Instead of asking whether your BMI is normal, ask: do my habits support my body? Do I move enough, sleep enough, eat reasonably? Numbers can mislead, but habits rarely lie. Focus on what you can control today.

articles.title: BMI for Children and Teens: Don't Use Adult Categories
articles.summary: Children's bodies are still growing, so adult BMI categories don't apply. What's used instead is age-based BMI percentiles.
articles.content_md:
## Why the categories differ

Adult BMI categories (18.5 / 25 / 30) were built from data on adults whose bodies have finished growing. Children and teens are still growing: their body composition changes fast with age and puberty stages. Applying adult cutoffs to a growing body isn't just inaccurate — it can mislead.

## What's actually used: age-based BMI percentiles

For children aged 2 and up, health professionals use age-and-sex-specific BMI growth charts. The result is read as a percentile: the 85th percentile, for example, means the child's BMI is higher than 85 percent of kids their age. This compares a child with peers their age, not with adults.

## Don't self-diagnose

Percentile charts are clinical tools. Reading them needs context: the child's growth history, family eating patterns, activity, and other factors. If you're worried about your child's weight, the right move is a conversation with a pediatrician or nutritionist — not judgment from a single number.

## For parents: watch your language

This matters. Children who get teased about weight — even as a joke — are at risk of body image issues and unhealthy eating patterns later in life. Keep the conversation focused on healthy family habits: eating together, moving together, sleeping enough. Not on the child's scale number.

## When to see a professional

Consult promptly if there's a drastic, unexplained weight change, or if the child shows signs of disordered eating. Early detection is always better, and treatment is the domain of professionals, not apps.

## What families can do

The home environment has huge influence. Keep fruit and water easy to reach, limit sugary drinks at home without drama, and get kids moving in fun ways — ball games, cycling, evening walks together. Enough sleep matters too, since poor sleep is linked to messy eating patterns. It's all about family habits, not monitoring a child's plate under a microscope.

## Focus on growing, not shrinking

The language adults use around children shapes how kids see their own bodies. Avoid commenting on anyone's body shape in front of children — including your own. A child who grows up with a healthy relationship to food and their body has something far more valuable than a perfect percentile number.

articles.title: Muscle vs Fat: Why Two People With the Same BMI Can Be Worlds Apart
articles.summary: A kilo of muscle and a kilo of fat weigh the same — but they tell very different health stories.
articles.content_md:
## Picture this

Imagine two people: both 75 kg and 175 cm, so their BMI is exactly the same, 24.5. One lifts weights three times a week; the other is completely sedentary. The scale numbers are twins, but one has a dense, muscular build and the other has high body fat. That's BMI's blind spot: it sees weight, not what's inside it.

## Why athletes can be "overweight"

Muscle is denser than fat — smaller in volume for the same weight. A muscular person can easily land in the BMI overweight category despite low body fat and great physical capacity. This isn't BMI being broken; it was never BMI's job to begin with.

## What matters more than the scale

If you train regularly, watch things other than the scale: a shrinking waistline, clothes fitting better, not getting winded climbing stairs, and training loads slowly going up. Those are all progress signals that one BMI number can't capture.

## Strength training for beginners

The good news: building muscle doesn't require a fancy gym. Two to three sessions a week with your own bodyweight — squats, push-ups, planks — is enough for beginners. Start light, keep good form, add gradually. Added muscle also helps your metabolism and everyday posture.

## A note of caution

This article isn't medical training advice. If you have specific health conditions — heart, joints, or you're pregnant — discuss your training plans with a professional before starting.

## Scale going up even though you train?

This is the classic beginner trap: you start strength training, eat more regularly, but the scale goes up a kilo or two. Don't panic yet. In the early phase, your body can add muscle while losing fat at the same time — total weight may stall or rise slightly while your body composition is actually improving. That's why the mirror, the tape measure, and better-fitting clothes are fairer judges than the scale alone.

## Be patient with the process

Building muscle is slow — think months, not weeks. But every training session is a deposit. As long as your waistline isn't growing and your strength is increasing, you're on the right track even if your BMI number isn't moving anywhere.

articles.title: Waist Circumference: The Cheap and Easy Companion to BMI
articles.summary: Fat around the belly carries higher risk — and measuring it only takes a tape measure.
articles.content_md:
## Why the belly gets the spotlight

Not all fat is created equal. Fat stored around the internal organs of the belly (visceral fat) is linked to higher metabolic risk than fat on the hips or thighs. BMI can't see where your fat is stored — that's where waist circumference helps.

## How to measure correctly

Stand straight and relaxed, wrap the tape around the midpoint between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone. Keep the tape level, not pressing into the skin, and measure after a normal exhale — not while holding your breath or sucking in your stomach. Be honest; nobody's judging.

## The cutoffs

WHO uses these benchmarks for adult populations: risk starts rising at a waist circumference of 94 cm and above for men and 80 cm and above for women, with even higher risk at 102 cm and 88 cm. Remember, these are population screening benchmarks — your trend over time matters as much as the number itself.

## Not a replacement, a companion

Waist circumference doesn't replace BMI; it complements it. Together they paint a more honest picture: BMI speaks to weight relative to height, waist circumference speaks to fat distribution. Both are cheap, fast, and doable at home.

## When to consult someone

If your waist measurement is far above the cutoff and stays there, or keeps rising over months, use that as a reason to talk to a health professional — not to panic. The data you've collected actually makes that consultation far more productive.

## How often to measure

No need to do it daily — waist circumference changes far more slowly than body weight. Once a month is enough, under the same conditions (morning, before eating). Record it in the same place as your weight notes so it's easy to compare.

## Track it alongside BMI

The most practical combo for most people: BMI from Raga plus waist circumference once a month. If your BMI is dropping and your waistline is shrinking, that's a strong signal you're losing fat, not just water or muscle. Two simple numbers, a much fuller story.
